anomalies1i.title: Origin at the Local Standard of Rest (the 'buoy at rest')
anomalies1i.observation: Before entering the solar system, 'Oumuamua was moving at only ~10 km/s relative to the Local Standard of Rest (LSR): its heliocentric velocity was (U,V,W) = (-11.5, -22.4, -7.7) km/s (26.32 km/s total), which in the LSR frame leaves negligible radial (U) and vertical (W) galactic motion and only a ~11 km/s lag in the rotational (V) component. Mamajek (arXiv:1710.11364, submitted Oct 31, 2017) computed that its velocity sat within 5 km/s of the median UVW velocity of local field stars and that fewer than ~1 in 500 field stars in the solar neighborhood have velocities so close to that local median (essentially the LSR). The Sun itself moves faster relative to the LSR (~18 km/s peculiar motion) than 'Oumuamua did.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Loeb argued this is exactly where you would park an artificial object meant to survey passing stars — or to hide its origin: in 'Six Strange Facts about 'Oumuamua' (arXiv:1811.08832, Nov 2018) he noted only one star in 500 moves as slowly in the LSR frame and called the LSR 'the ideal frame for camouflage,' avoiding association with any particular star. In 'Extraterrestrial' (2021) he counted the ~1-in-500 kinematic coincidence among the improbabilities any natural ejection model must explain, since ejected rocks inherit their parent star's velocity plus an ejection kick — 'Oumuamua was effectively at rest in the galactic frame and the solar system ran into it.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: Young objects ejected at low velocity from nearby young stellar systems naturally cluster near the LSR before gravitational scattering ('disk heating') ages their kinematics; the low LSR velocity implies 'Oumuamua is dynamically young (<~100 Myr — Hallatt & Wiegert 2020, arXiv:1911.02473, AJ; Hsieh, Laughlin & Arce 2021 linked it to the ~30 Myr Carina moving group and a molecular-cloud origin, arXiv:2105.14670, ApJ). The ISSI team (Nature Astronomy 3, 594, 2019) treated the kinematics as pointing to a young planetesimal population, not design.
anomalies1i.loeb_quote: Perhaps 'Oumuamua was like a buoy resting in the expanse of the universe, and our solar system was like a ship that ran into it at high speed.
anomalies1i.quote_source: Avi Loeb, 'Extraterrestrial' (2021) — verbatim; same buoy-and-ship analogy repeated in 2019-2021 interviews. The LSR/1-in-500 'camouflage' argument is in 'Six Strange Facts about 'Oumuamua' (arXiv:1811.08832; Scientific American, Nov 20, 2018).
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: Minor corrections only; the entry was substantively accurate. (1) Date CONFIRMED exactly: Mamajek arXiv:1710.11364 v1 submitted 2017-10-31. (2) Numbers CONFIRMED: heliocentric U,V,W = (-11.457, -22.395, -7.746) km/s (26.32 km/s total); LSR-frame motion ~10 km/s dominated by a ~11 km/s lag in V with negligible U/W; the '<1 in 500 field stars' figure is verbatim from Mamajek, though he phrased it as stars 'so close to the median UVW velocity' of local stars (within 5 km/s of the median) — wording tightened. Sun's peculiar motion (~18 km/s) > 'Oumuamua's ~10 km/s is true. (3) Quote UPGRADED from paraphrase to verified verbatim from Extraterrestrial (2021): 'Perhaps Oumuamua was like a buoy resting in the expanse of the universe, and our solar system was like a ship that ran into it at high speed.' Attribution fixed: the buoy analogy is from the book/interviews; arXiv:1811.08832 ('Six Strange Facts', submitted 2018-11-21, also Scientific American 2018-11-20) carries the LSR/1-in-500 item, which Loeb there frames as 'the ideal frame for camouflage'. (4) Official explanation CONFIRMED and fairly stated: Hallatt & Wiegert 2020 (arXiv:1911.02473, AJ — low LSR velocity implies age <~100 Myr) and Hsieh, Laughlin & Arce 2021 (arXiv:2105.14670, ApJ — ~30 Myr Carina moving group / molecular-cloud origin); ISSI team citation Nature Astronomy 3, 594 (2019) is correct. Added arXiv:1911.02473 and the Scientific American essay to sources. (5) Nothing invented or conflated beyond the two attribution nits.

anomalies1i.title: Extreme lightcurve elongation (~10x brightness swings)
anomalies1i.observation: Meech et al. (Nature 552, 378; published 2017-11-20 with ESO release eso1737) reported brightness variations by a factor of ~10 (about 2.5 magnitudes) every ~7.3 hours as the object rotated. The original fit implied an axis ratio of up to ~10:1; later reanalyses accounting for phase-angle effects put the most likely aspect ratio at ~6:1 (6±1) — still more elongated than any of the hundreds of thousands of asteroids and comets ever measured in the solar system (typical bodies are ~2:1 or 3:1).
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Loeb repeatedly listed the record-setting elongation as strange fact number one: no known solar-system body comes close, and an extreme aspect ratio is what an artificial thin structure (cigar or disc seen edge-on) would produce. In 'Six Strange Facts' (arXiv:1811.08832, also published in Scientific American on 2018-11-20) he noted the shape inference, combined with the later acceleration anomaly, pushed him toward a thin-membrane geometry rather than a rocky ellipsoid.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: Natural shaping mechanisms proposed: tidal fragmentation of a body during a close stellar or planetary encounter can spin off highly elongated splinters (Zhang & Lin, Nature Astronomy, April 2020, reproduced ~10:1 and even more elongated fragments); prolonged interstellar-dust erosion or collisional grinding can also elongate small bodies. The ISSI team (Nature Astronomy 3, 594, 2019) called the shape unusual but consistent with a purely natural origin, noting that lightcurve amplitude is enhanced at the observed phase angles (19-27 deg), softening the required ratio to ~6:1; McNeill et al. (2018) independently derived 6±1 from lightcurve inversion, and Vazan & Sari (MNRAS 493, 1546, 2020) argued irregular surface reflection properties could mimic part of the amplitude, allowing an even less elongated body.
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: Verified against Nature/ESO/arXiv primary sources. (1) Date CONFIRMED: Nature paper and ESO eso1737 both 2017-11-20. (2) Numbers CONFIRMED: factor-of-10 (~2.5 mag) variation, ~7.3 h period, original ~10:1 description, later ~6:1 (ISSI: '6±1:1 most likely after accounting for phase-angle effects'; McNeill et al. 2018: 6±1; Zhang & Lin, Nature Astronomy 2020-04-13, real and produces >=10:1 tidal fragments). (3) No quote present; Loeb 'Six Strange Facts' arXiv:1811.08832 confirmed real and correctly characterized. (4) One CONFLATION fixed: the original entry attributed the amplitude-softening to 'tumbling geometry' by 'McNeill et al. and Vazan & Sari'. Actually the softening from ~10:1 to >=6:1 comes from phase-angle amplitude enhancement (ISSI team, observed phase angles 19-27 deg); McNeill et al. 2018 got 6±1 via lightcurve inversion; Vazan & Sari (MNRAS 493, 1546, 2020; arXiv:2001.09283) argued irregular SURFACE REFLECTION properties, not tumbling, could allow a less elongated shape. Also tightened observation wording ('at least 6:1' -> most-likely 6±1 after phase-angle correction) and added Zhang & Lin and Vazan & Sari URLs to sources. ISSI wording adjusted from 'within reach of natural processes' to their actual conclusion 'consistent with a purely natural origin'.

anomalies1i.title: Complex tumbling (non-principal-axis rotation)
anomalies1i.observation: Photometry from multiple telescopes could not be phased to a single rotation period; Fraser et al. (Nature Astronomy, arXiv 2017-11-30, published 2018-02-09) and Drahus et al. (Nature Astronomy 2018, Gemini North data) showed 'Oumuamua is tumbling — rotating in an excited non-principal-axis state with lightcurve periodicities near ~7.3-8.7 h (Drahus: ~7.34 h average; Belton: 8.67 h). Belton et al. (ApJL 856, L21, April 2018) formalized the spin-state families from 818 observations over 29.3 days. Fraser et al. computed a damping timescale for the tumbling of at least a billion years, so it likely tumbled through interstellar space since a violent event (e.g. a collision) long before reaching us.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Loeb counted the excited spin as another oddity constraining natural origins (a collision or fragmentation is needed to set it tumbling) and argued the tumbling made the outgassing explanation for the acceleration harder: citing Rafikov (2018), he noted that cometary jets should have torqued the object and rapidly changed its spin — Rafikov showed outgassing strong enough to supply the acceleration would drive spin evolution within days (even rotational breakup) unless the jet's torque lever arm was finely tuned, yet no spin change or sudden kicks were observed. Separately, Loeb cited Mashchenko's (2019) lightcurve-torque modeling approvingly for its conclusion that the shape is disc-like at ~91% confidence — though Mashchenko's own best fit (a thin disc under moderate outgassing torque of comet-like amplitude) actually supports the natural-comet reading.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: Tumbling is common among small solar-system bodies after collisions; Fraser et al. attributed it to a collision in 'Oumuamua's birth system before or during ejection. Belton et al. showed several spin states fit the data, including ones consistent with either cigar or pancake shapes. Rafikov (2018) argued the observed spin stability limits any outgassing torques — a point against the comet interpretation — but later modeling (Mashchenko 2019; Seligman et al.) showed outgassing concentrated at the substellar point can supply the acceleration while leaving the tumbling period essentially unchanged.
anomalies1i.loeb_quote: showing no change in spin or sudden kicks as routinely observed from localized jets
anomalies1i.quote_source: Loeb, 'On the Possibility of an Artificial Origin for `Oumuamua', Astrobiology review (lweb.cfa.harvard.edu/~loeb/Loeb_Astrobiology.pdf), citing Rafikov 2018
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: Core facts all verified (date within window; Fraser arXiv 2017-11-30 / Nature Astronomy 2018-02-09; Drahus ~7.34 h; Belton ApJL 856 L21 April 2018, DOI aab370; billion-year damping timescale is Fraser et al.'s own statement; all four source URLs resolve to the claimed papers, with the fourth being Mashchenko 2019 MNRAS 489, 3003, arXiv:1906.03696). Two fixes: (1) loeb_take conflated three claims — the 'very finely tuned outgassing' argument belongs to Rafikov (2018: fine tuning of the jet's torque lever arm needed to avoid rapid spin evolution 'on a timescale of a few days'), not to Mashchenko, whose own 'fine-tuning problem' wording refers to cigar-shaped models (16% probability) vs disc models (91%); Loeb cited Mashchenko approvingly for the ~90%-confidence disc-like shape, and Mashchenko's fitted torque was actually comet-like in amplitude (supporting the natural interpretation). Reworded loeb_take accordingly. (2) official_explanation's 'used both for and against' clause sharpened: Rafikov's spin-stability point argued against the outgassing interpretation; later substellar-point outgassing models (Seligman et al.) reconciled stable spin with jets. Also added a verified short Loeb quote (extracted directly from his Astrobiology review PDF) to the previously empty loeb_quote field, and added the Rafikov ApJL DOI link to sources.

anomalies1i.title: Breakthrough Listen radio silence
anomalies1i.observation: On 2017-12-13 (3:45-9:45 pm ET) Breakthrough Listen observed 'Oumuamua with the Green Bank Telescope across four bands (L, S, X, C; 1.1-11.6 GHz), accumulating ~90 TB of raw data over the 2-hour on-source observation plus calibration scans. No artificial narrowband signals were found. The published analysis (Enriquez et al. 2018, Res. Notes AAS 2, 9) set limits sensitive to omnidirectional transmitters with power as low as ~0.08 W — a fraction of a cellphone — at the object's distance.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Loeb (who chairs Breakthrough Starshot's advisory committee) endorsed the search and treated the null result as consistent with, not fatal to, the artifact hypothesis: a defunct piece of technological debris or a passive lightsail need not transmit. In 'Extraterrestrial' he argued most artifacts we encounter would likely be dead 'space junk' of other civilizations, so radio silence carries limited evidential weight.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: The mainstream reading is straightforward: a natural rock does not transmit, and the deep non-detection removed the most testable technosignature prediction. The SETI Institute's Allen Telescope Array had already observed it 2017-11-23 to 12-05 (Harp et al. 2019, Acta Astronautica) and independently found no signals down to ~10 W EIRP at 1 GHz (rising to ~100 W at 7 GHz), and the ISSI team's Nature Astronomy review found no compelling evidence for an artificial origin, citing the radio quiet as consistent with a natural body.
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: Two minor corrections; everything else verified. (1) Date/time exact: Breakthrough Listen's first block ran 3:45-9:45 pm ET on 2017-12-13 at GBT (breakthroughinitiatives.org/news/15). (2) Numbers: L/S/X/C bands, 1.1-11.6 GHz, and the 0.08 W transmitter limit confirmed verbatim against Enriquez et al. (arXiv:1801.02814, RNAAS 2, 9, DOI 10.3847/2515-5172/aaa6c9). Nuance fixed: the 90 TB was accumulated over the 2-hour on-source observation of 'Oumuamua (plus calibration), not the whole 6-hour block. ERROR fixed: the Harp et al. 2019 ATA limit is not a flat ~10 W — the corrected published version (a Jansky-to-EIRP calculation error was fixed in revision) gives ~10 W EIRP at 1 GHz rising to ~100 W at 7 GHz; also the ATA observations (2017-11-23 to 12-05) preceded the GBT session, so phrasing adjusted so it doesn't read as a follow-up. (3) loeb_quote is empty — nothing to verify; loeb_take is a fair paraphrase (Loeb chairing the Breakthrough Starshot advisory committee confirmed via CfA news; 'debris from advanced technological equipment' framing is genuine Bialy & Loeb 2018 language and the space-junk argument appears in Extraterrestrial). (4) Official explanation fairly stated and backed by real papers (Enriquez 2018; Harp 2019; ISSI 'Oumuamua Team, Nature Astronomy 2019 — 'no compelling evidence' for artificial origin). (5) Nothing invented or conflated; all three original source URLs are real, and I added the two arXiv links to the sources list.

anomalies1i.title: Population density too high for ejected rocks
anomalies1i.observation: Scaling from Pan-STARRS's single detection, Do, Tucker & Tonry (ApJL 855, L10, published 2018-03-06) inferred a space density of 'Oumuamua-like objects of ~0.2 per AU^3 — a mass density of ~4 Earth masses of ejecta per cubic parsec, requiring each star to account for over 10^16 ejected bodies. The required planetesimal disk mass exceeds all estimates of the solar system's own planetesimal disk by an order of magnitude; Loeb noted the density is 2-8 orders of magnitude above the pre-detection prediction of Moro-Martin, Turner & Loeb (2009), and rounded the requirement to ~10^15 (a quadrillion) objects per star.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Loeb ('Six Strange Facts', arXiv:1811.08832, and book 'Extraterrestrial') argued each star would need to eject ~10^15 'Oumuamua-like objects — 2-8 orders of magnitude more than he and Moro-Martin had predicted in 2009 — an implausible budget if they are random rocks. A random population of 10^15 solar sails per star is equally unreasonable, so he argued targeted trajectories 'add explanatory power': far fewer artifacts are needed if they aim for the habitable zones of stars rather than sampling all orbits randomly. Separately, Siraj & Loeb (New Astronomy 2022) ran the same mass-budget attack against the nitrogen-iceberg model, and Loeb repeatedly cited Moro-Martin's 2018-2019 finding that ejection scenarios fall short.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: The ISSI team (Bannister et al., Nature Astronomy 2019) countered that with a single detected object there are no firm constraints on the size-frequency distribution, so the measured number density cannot be converted to a mass density: plausible SFDs with a few percent of mass in ~50 m fragments match the observed density with only 0.02-15 Earth masses ejected per star, making the 'higher than expected' claim unsupported. Do et al. themselves proposed Oort-cloud shedding by post-main-sequence stars as a supplementary source; Zhang & Lin (2020) and Desch & Jackson (2021) each predict abundant small fragments. Moro-Martin (2018, 2019), however, found the tension persists under many assumptions — the debate hinged on the unknown size distribution, which detections of 2I and 3I are only now starting to constrain (km-scale ISOs are far rarer, ~10^-4 to 10^-2 per AU^3).
anomalies1i.loeb_quote: Each star in the Milky-Way needs to eject 10^15 such objects during its lifetime to account for the inferred population, much more than anticipated based on the Solar System.
anomalies1i.quote_source: Loeb, 'Six Strange Facts about 'Oumuamua', arXiv:1811.08832 (Nov 2018; also Scientific American, 2018-11-20)
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: Date 2018-03-06 CONFIRMED exact (ApJL publication date). Density 0.2 au^-3 and ~4 M-earth/pc^3 confirmed verbatim. THREE corrections: (1) Do et al. state 'each star must account for over 10^16 ejected bodies', not ~10^15 — the quadrillion-per-star figure is Loeb's rounding in Six Strange Facts, now attributed correctly; Do et al.'s own stated excess is 'an order of magnitude' over solar-system planetesimal-disk estimates, while the '2-8 orders of magnitude above prediction' comparison is Loeb's, versus Moro-Martin, Turner & LOEB 2009 (Loeb co-authored the prediction — 'Moro-Martin's own tension' framing fixed). (2) Official explanation misattributed: Moro-Martin 2018/2019 CONFIRMED the tension rather than resolving it; the actual rebuttal is the ISSI team's size-frequency-distribution argument ('with a single detected object there are no firm constraints... the claim that the observed number density is higher than expected... is not supported'), not primarily Poisson error; 'later surveys refining density downward' softened to an SFD-constraint statement since 3I-era densities (~10^-4-10^-2 au^-3) apply to km-scale objects. (3) Added verified verbatim Loeb quote from arXiv:1811.08832 with source; added Moro-Martin 2019 (arXiv:1811.00023) to sources. Loeb's targeted-mission corollary verified verbatim ('the required numbers could be reduced dramatically if...special orbits that dive into the innermost, habitable regions').

anomalies1i.title: Non-gravitational acceleration with no visible coma or tail
anomalies1i.observation: Micheli et al. (Nature 559, 223; published 2018-06-27) detected, at ~30-sigma significance, a non-gravitational acceleration of 'Oumuamua of 4.92 +/- 0.16 x 10^-6 m/s^2 at 1 AU, pointed radially away from the Sun and falling off roughly as 1/r^2. Yet deep imaging (VLT, HST, Gemini) and Spitzer showed no coma, no dust tail, and no detected gas — the usual engine of such accelerations in comets. Explaining it with outgassing would need ~10 kg/s of gas with a gas-to-dust ratio >100x any known comet.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: This is the anomaly that launched the artifact hypothesis: an excess sunward-decaying push with no visible propellant is precisely the signature of solar radiation pressure on a thin, low-mass-per-area object. Loeb called the combination of acceleration plus no coma the single most anomalous fact about 'Oumuamua, and in later essays assigned the natural-comet explanation a low likelihood given the additional fine-tuning (no spin-up torque, no infrared detection) it requires.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: Micheli et al. themselves concluded comet-like outgassing is physically viable if 'Oumuamua has unusual thermal/compositional properties (large grains, low dust). The ISSI team (Nature Astronomy 2019) endorsed volatile outgassing below detection thresholds. Dedicated exotic-ice models followed: hydrogen iceberg (Seligman & Laughlin, ApJL 896, L8, 2020), nitrogen-ice fragment (Desch & Jackson, JGR Planets, 2021), and radiolytic H2 trapped in water ice (Bergner & Seligman, Nature 615, 610, March 2023). A minority view (Katz 2019, arXiv:1904.02218) disputed the acceleration itself, but the 30-sigma detection is broadly accepted.
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: All claims verified against primary sources; no corrections required. (1) Date exact: Nature 559, 223-226 published 2018-06-27. (2) Acceleration (4.92 +/- 0.16) x 10^-6 m/s^2 confirmed verbatim; ratio = 30.8 so ~30-sigma is accurate; radially anti-solar ~1/r^2 confirmed; ~10 kg/s is Micheli et al.'s own adopted best estimate (their stated range 0.7-140 kg/s); the 'gas-to-dust ratio >100x any known comet' figure is Katz's (arXiv:1904.02218 / Ap&SS 364, 51, 2019) explicit calculation ('at least 100 times greater than that of known Solar System comets') — Katz is already cited in sources, so the claim is grounded, though a pedant could attribute it to Katz explicitly. (3) loeb_quote empty, nothing to verify; loeb_take is fair paraphrase of documented Loeb positions (Bialy & Loeb 2018 ApJL radiation-pressure sail 0.3-0.9 mm; repeated citation of 30-sigma acceleration + no coma as central anomaly; spin-up and Spitzer fine-tuning arguments). (4) Official explanation fairly stated with real papers: Micheli et al. attribute to comet-like outgassing; ISSI team = Nature Astronomy 3, 594-602 (2019), DOI 10.1038/s41550-019-0816-x, matches source URL; Seligman & Laughlin ApJL 896, L8 (2020) H2 ice confirmed; Desch & Jackson JGR Planets 126, e2020JE006807 (March 2021) N2 ice confirmed; Bergner & Seligman Nature 615, 610 (22 March 2023), DOI s41586-022-05687-w confirmed and matches source URL 4. (5) Nothing invented or conflated; all four source URLs resolve to the claimed papers.

anomalies1i.title: Bialy-Loeb lightsail hypothesis (the 0.3-0.9 mm sail)
anomalies1i.observation: Bialy & Loeb (ApJL 868, L1; arXiv 2018-10-26, published 2018-11-12) showed that solar radiation pressure alone reproduces the observed 1/r^2 excess acceleration (Micheli et al. 2018) if 'Oumuamua's mass-to-area ratio is ~0.1 g/cm^2 - i.e., a thin sheet only ~0.3-0.9 mm thick for normal material densities. They calculated such a thin film would survive interstellar dust/gas ablation and tidal/centrifugal (tensile) stresses over galactic distances.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: The paper offered two readings: a naturally produced ultra-thin object of a new class, or an artificial origin - 'a lightsail, floating in interstellar space as debris from advanced technological equipment' - with a 'more exotic' alternative that it was a deliberate probe. Loeb expanded this into 'Extraterrestrial' (Jan 2021), arguing the artifact hypothesis was the most economical explanation of all the anomalies jointly and publicly calling artificial origin a 'serious possibility'; in his August 2025 Loeb Scale paper (arXiv:2508.09167) he retroactively ranked 'Oumuamua Level 4 ('critical threshold' - technological explanation must be considered), versus Level 0 for 2I/Borisov and Level 4 for 3I/ATLAS.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: Curran (A&A 649, L17, 2021, ''Oumuamua as a light sail: Evidence against artificial origin') showed light sails asymptotically approach a terminal velocity, so a sail with 'Oumuamua's parameters (thickness <~1 mm, mass ~4x10^4 kg) would need roughly half a billion years just to reach the Sun from its closest likely system of origin - making an artificial sail very unlikely. Zhou et al. (A&A 667, A108, 2022) added that a tumbling sail is inconsistent with the data: <1.5% probability of matching the observed lightcurve amplitude and ~0.4% probability of remaining visible in all 55 post-discovery observations. The ISSI team (Nature Astronomy, 2019) found all observations consistent with a purely natural origin, and porous fractal-aggregate models (Moro-Martin 2019; Luu, Flekkoy & Toussaint 2020) offered a natural route to lightsail-like area-to-mass ratios.
anomalies1i.loeb_quote: Alternatively, a more exotic scenario is that 'Oumuamua may be a fully operational probe sent intentionally to Earth vicinity by an alien civilization.
anomalies1i.quote_source: Bialy & Loeb 2018, ApJL 868, L1 ('Could Solar Radiation Pressure Explain 'Oumuamua's Peculiar Acceleration?'), Section 5 - exact sentence verified against the published text
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: Date and physics confirmed exactly (arXiv 2018-10-26; ApJL 868 L1 published 2018-11-12; m/A ~0.1 g/cm^2; 0.3-0.9 mm sheet; dust/gas and tensile-stress survival analysis in paper). Three fixes: (1) loeb_quote was a silent truncation - restored the full sentence beginning "Alternatively, a more exotic scenario is that..."; the paper's actual lightsail wording ("a lightsail, floating in interstellar space as debris from advanced technological equipment") substituted for the invented phrase "a lightsail of artificial origin". (2) official_explanation conflated papers: Curran 2021 (A&A 649, L17) argues terminal-velocity/travel-time (~0.5 Gyr from nearest plausible origin) and extreme thinness/mass constraints, NOT tumbling; the tumbling/brightness-modulation argument is Zhou et al. 2022 (A&A 667, A108: <1.5% lightcurve-amplitude match, 0.4% visibility probability) - both now correctly attributed, Zhou added to sources. (3) "publicly estimated better-than-even personal odds" is unsourced - no >50% Loeb statement found; replaced with documented "serious possibility" framing and his book's most-economical-hypothesis argument, plus his Aug 2025 retroactive Loeb Scale Level 4 ranking of 1I (arXiv:2508.09167; 2I=0, 3I/ATLAS=4).

anomalies1i.title: Spitzer infrared non-detection: small and shiny
anomalies1i.observation: Spitzer stared at 'Oumuamua's position for 30.2 hours at 4.5 microns (IRAC channel 2) on 2017-11-21/22 UT and saw nothing, with a 3-sigma flux upper limit of 0.3 microJy (Trilling et al., AJ 156, 261; published 2018-11-14). This caps the effective spherical diameter at <98, <140, or <440 m (for low/middle/high thermal beaming) and forces the albedo above 0.2, 0.1, or 0.01 respectively — plus tight 3-sigma upper limits on outgassing: CO2 < 9e22 and CO < ~9e21 molecules/s.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Loeb highlighted that the preferred solutions make 'Oumuamua small and at least ~10x more reflective than typical solar-system comets and asteroids — consistent with a polished metallic or icy-clean artificial surface — while the CO/CO2 limits simultaneously starve the outgassing explanation for the acceleration of its most common propellants. Smaller size also means the non-gravitational push acted on a lower-mass object, easing the radiation-pressure requirement.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: Trilling et al. proposed that if 'Oumuamua is a comet-like body, low-level post-perihelion volatile emission after its 0.256 AU perihelion passage could have deposited a fresh, bright icy mantle, explaining the high albedo; water vapor (invisible at 4.5 microns, ~6e25 molecules/s needed) could still drive the acceleration. The nitrogen-ice model (Jackson & Desch 2021) naturally yields a high albedo (~0.64, N2 frost like Pluto's surface) and a small body (~45 x 44 x 7.5 m), fitting Spitzer's limits, as does the hydrogen-iceberg model.
anomalies1i._verifyNotes: All core facts verified against primary sources — date (AJ published exactly 2018-11-14), 30.2 hr / 4.5 um / 2017-11-21-22 UT, 0.3 uJy 3-sigma limit, diameter <98/<140/<440 m, albedo >0.2/>0.1/>0.01, and real CO/CO2 limits (now quantified: CO2 < 9e22, CO < ~9e21 molec/s from the paper). Three minor fixes: (1) citation attribution — the nitrogen-ice paper at DOI 10.1029/2020JE006706 is Jackson & Desch 2021 (Paper I), not 'Desch & Jackson'; also added their derived dimensions 45x44x7.5 m. (2) official_explanation mechanism reworded from 'ice-scoured' to the paper's actual proposal: post-perihelion volatile emission depositing a fresh bright icy mantle; added Trilling's ~6e25 H2O molecules/s figure. (3) loeb_take 'up to ~10x' tightened to 'at least ~10x' to match Loeb's actual claim in 'Six Strange Facts' / Extraterrestrial. Empty loeb_quote is fine (nothing fabricated). Replaced the NAU press-release link (redundant) with arXiv:1811.08072 and the JPL 2018-11-14 release.

anomalies1i.title: Pancake, not cigar: the 91% oblate fit
anomalies1i.observation: Mashchenko (MNRAS 489, 3003; arXiv:1906.03696, submitted 9 June 2019) fit the full October-November 2017 lightcurve with a physical tumbling-plus-torque model and found disc-shaped (oblate) bodies reproduce the deep brightness minima with 91% likelihood, versus only 16% for cigar shapes, which additionally suffer an orientation fine-tuning problem. The best-fit body is a thin slab of ~115 x 111 x 19 m — an aspect ratio near 6:6:1 (assumed geometric albedo 0.1) — under a modest outgassing torque whose amplitude, relative to the non-gravitational acceleration, matches Solar System comets.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Loeb seized on this: the popular cigar was an artist's conception, while the data statistically favor a flat pancake at 91% confidence — far closer to a sail geometry. In essays and in 'Extraterrestrial' he emphasized that a razor-thin disc is even harder to make naturally than a cigar (Mashchenko's fits even allow a millimeter-thin sheet), and — following Rafikov's 2018 argument that outgassing torques should have measurably spun the object up — that the required torque balance further strains the invisible-outgassing story. The 2025 Loeb Scale paper (arXiv:2508.09167) again cites 1I's 'extreme geometry' among the accumulated anomalies justifying its Level 4 ranking.

Nitrogen fragment (Jackson & Desch / Desch & Jackson, JGR Planets 126, 2021) vs Siraj & Loeb (New Astronomy 92, 101730, 2022): the required exo-Pluto mass of heavy elements exceeds the total locked in all stars (95% confidence). anomalies1i.title: Retroactive Loeb Scale rank: Level 4
anomalies1i.observation: In 'The Loeb Scale: Astronomical Classification of Interstellar Objects' (Eldadi, Tenenbaum & Loeb, arXiv:2508.09167, submitted Aug 6, 2025; later published in the International Journal of Astrobiology as the 'Interstellar Object Significance Scale (IOSS)'), Loeb and coauthors defined a 0-10 anomaly scale extending the Torino Scale framework (levels 0-3 natural, 4-7 increasingly anomalous, 8-10 confirmed artificial) and retroactively scored the known interstellar objects: 1I/'Oumuamua = Level 4, 2I/Borisov = Level 0, 3I/ATLAS = Level 4 (at the time of writing). A follow-up, 'Quantitative Mapping of the Loeb Scale' (Trivedi & Loeb, arXiv:2509.06253, Sep 2025), formalized the scoring numerically, explicitly modeled on Sagan's quantification of the Kardashev scale.
anomalies1i.loeb_take: Level 4 marks 'Oumuamua as genuinely anomalous — multiple independent deviations from any known natural class (non-gravitational acceleration without a coma of gas or dust, extreme geometry, spectral properties unexplained by conventional models) — while Borisov's Level 0 shows the scale is not alien-hype: a normal comet scores zero. Loeb used the 1I-vs-2I contrast throughout 2025-2026 essays as the template for judging 3I/ATLAS, arguing anomaly-scoring should be systematic rather than dismissed case-by-case.
anomalies1i.official_explanation: The scale is Loeb's framework, not community consensus — though it did pass peer review (published in the International Journal of Astrobiology). Critics note the ISSI 'Oumuamua team's 2019 Nature Astronomy paper ('The Natural History of 'Oumuamua') already found no compelling evidence to favor an alien explanation, and that anomaly scales with author-controlled thresholds risk baking in the author's priors. No IAU or NASA body has adopted the scale; mainstream papers continue to classify 1I as a natural (if unusual) planetesimal and 3I/ATLAS as an active comet.
anomalies1i.loeb_quote: [paraphrase] On the Loeb scale, 'Oumuamua ranks at Level 4 — the critical threshold, anomalous enough to warrant enhanced follow-up — while Borisov, a classical comet despite its interstellar origin, ranks Level 0.

anomalies2i.title: Extreme carbon-monoxide enrichment — the most CO-rich comet measured inside 2.5 AU
anomalies2i.observation: Two independent teams reported on 2I/Borisov's coma in the weeks after its 2019-12-08 perihelion (q = 2.0065 AU, e = 3.3565). Bodewits et al. (HST/COS ultraviolet, four post-perihelion epochs from 2019-12-11 to 2020-01-13) derived Q(CO) = 6.4–10.7 × 10^26 molecules s^-1 (equivalent to 30–50 kg s^-1) and CO/H2O of at least 173% — 'more than three times higher than previously measured for any comet in the inner (<2.5 au) solar system,' where CO/H2O mostly ranges 0.2–23% with typical values near 4%. Simultaneous Swift/UVOT + HST/COS epochs (2019-12-19/22 and 2020-01-13) gave CO/H2O = 130–155% directly. Cordiner et al. (ALMA, 2019-12-15/16) measured Q(CO) = (4.4 ± 0.7) × 10^26 s^-1 and Q(HCN) = (7.0 ± 1.1) × 10^23 s^-1, giving CO/H2O ≈ 35–105%, HCN/H2O ≈ 0.06–0.16% (ordinary), and CO/HCN = 630 (+200/−340) — higher than any comet previously observed except the peculiar Oort Cloud comet C/2016 R2 (PanSTARRS), whose CO/HCN was 26,400 at rH = 2.8 AU. Excluding C/2016 R2, the next-highest CO/HCN was 238 ± 21 for C/2006 W3 (Christensen) at rH = 3.3 AU. The ALMA/NASA release put Borisov's CO abundance at 9–26× the solar-system comet average.
anomalies2i.loeb_take: Loeb has never treated Borisov's CO excess as a technosignature — it is chemistry, not engineering. In his retrospective framing Borisov is the one interstellar object that looked ordinary: a comet whose volatiles simply record a colder, more carbon-rich birth disk than the Sun's. In the 2025 Loeb Scale paper he co-authored (formally the Interstellar Object Significance Scale, IOSS; Eldadi, Tenenbaum & Loeb, arXiv:2508.09167, submitted 2025-08-06) Borisov is assigned Level 0 — fully consistent with natural processes — the lowest score of the three interstellar objects, against Level 4 for both 1I/'Oumuamua and 3I/ATLAS.
anomalies2i.official_explanation: Both teams read the CO excess as a formation-environment signature, not an anomaly. Cordiner et al.: Borisov 'must have formed in a relatively CO-rich environment — probably beyond the CO ice-line in the very cold, outer regions of a distant protoplanetary accretion disk, as part of a population of small, icy bodies analogous to our Solar System's own proto-Kuiper Belt.' Bodewits et al. add that the volatile carbon-to-oxygen ratio is 'nearly six times higher than that of previously measured solar system comets,' and derive three constraints on the host system: it must be chemically distinct from ours, Borisov must have formed beyond a CO snowline (with CO ice condensing alongside H2O rather than trapped in clathrate), and the system must have undergone dynamical stripping of planetesimals from beyond that snowline — an M-dwarf host, whose CO snowline sits near 6.6 AU, fits well. Bodewits et al. call the result 'the first glimpse into the ice content and chemical composition of the protoplanetary disk of another star that is substantially different from our own.' Notably, the papers do NOT treat known CO-rich solar-system comets as equivalent cases: Bodewits et al. explicitly exclude C/2016 R2 (PanSTARRS) from the comparison because its 2.6 AU perihelion meant it 'never reached the inner solar system where water sublimation is fully effective,' no H2O was detected in its coma, and its dominant volatile is most likely CO2 rather than CO. CO-driven comets outside 2.5 AU do commonly show CO exceeding H2O, so a CO-rich nucleus is not unprecedented in kind — but Borisov's ratio inside 2.5 AU, where water sublimation is fully effective, is the record.
anomalies2i.loeb_quote: Among the four interstellar objects, only Borisov appeared familiar. It was a comet, not much different from the analogous snowballs found in the Solar system.
anomalies2i.quote_source: Avi Loeb, 'The Unfamiliar Nature of Interstellar Objects,' Medium, 2022-09-23 (verified verbatim)

anomalies2i.title: Atomic nickel (and iron) vapor in a 180 K coma — and the solar-system comets that did the same thing
anomalies2i.observation: Guzik & Drahus (Nature 593, 375–378) detected gaseous atomic Ni I in Borisov's cold coma from VLT/X-shooter spectra taken 28, 30 and 31 January 2020 UT at a mean heliocentric distance of 2.322 AU (geocentric 2.064 AU) — equilibrium temperature ~180 K, far below the >700 K normally needed to vaporize metal-bearing dust. Production rate Q(Ni) = (0.9 ± 0.3) × 10^22 atoms s^-1, i.e. 0.002% of OH and 0.3% of CN, from a short-lived nickel-bearing parent with a 340 (+260/-200) s lifetime at 1 AU. Opitom et al. 2021 (A&A 650, L19; VLT/UVES, 12 epochs over ~21 h, 2019-11-15 to 2020-03-16, spanning 2.1 AU pre-perihelion to 2.6 AU post-perihelion) independently found Fe I and Ni I, measuring log(Ni I/Fe I) = 0.21 ± 0.18 for 2I against an average of -0.06 ± 0.31 for 17 solar-system comets — i.e. an ordinary ratio.
anomalies2i.loeb_take: Loeb explicitly uses Borisov as the metals baseline rather than an anomaly: he notes Borisov's Ni/Fe ratio matched ordinary comets, which is exactly why he treats 3I/ATLAS's early nickel-heavy, iron-poor plume as the outlier worth flagging. Under his own scale Borisov's metal chemistry contributes nothing to its Level 0 score.
anomalies2i.official_explanation: Published back-to-back in the same issue of Nature, Manfroid, Hutsemékers & Jehin (593, 372–374) showed the same phenomenon is ubiquitous at home: high-resolution UV-optical VLT/UVES spectra of about 20 solar-system comets collected since 2002 between 0.68 and 3.25 AU show up to about 40 Fe I and 25 Ni I emission lines, with Ni and Fe of the same order of magnitude (unlike the solar/meteoritic ratio, which runs ~10× more Fe). The paper weighs several release mechanisms — partial sublimation of Ni-rich sulfides such as pentlandite (needs >600 K), superheating of submicrometre fluffy aggregates, nanoparticle impact vapor (~1000 K) — and, on the strength of the Fe/Ni–carbon-oxide correlation, favors sublimation of low-temperature organometallic carriers, specifically the carbonyls Fe(CO)5 and Ni(CO)4, whose sublimation temperatures are only slightly above that of CO2 (later A&A work puts them near ~100 K, between CO2 and H2O); Ni(CO)4 sublimates ~10× faster than Fe(CO)5 near 300 K, which explains the cometary Ni overabundance. This pairing is the standard mainstream rebuttal invoked against the 3I/ATLAS 'nickel without iron' claim — and later VLT work (Hutsemékers et al. 2026, A&A 706, A43) showed 3I/ATLAS's log(Ni I/Fe I) fell from 1.27 ± 0.10 at 2.64 AU (the first epoch at which Fe I was detected at all; only lower limits, >0.99, exist at 3.78 and 3.14 AU) to ~0.3 near 1.9–2.0 AU, becoming indistinguishable from solar-system comets and from 2I/Borisov.
anomalies2i.loeb_quote: The interstellar comet 2I/Borisov showed nickel and iron with an abundance ratio that is similar to that observed in solar system comets.
anomalies2i.quote_source: Avi Loeb, 'New Data on the Extreme Nickel Production of 3I/ATLAS,' Medium, 2025-10-01

Both URLs retained but now correctly labeled; the A&A 652 L1 paper is in fact the correct source for the ~100 K carbonyl sublimation figure.

(3) FAIRNESS NUANCE in official_explanation — the Manfroid Nature paper presents carbonyls as ONE OF SEVERAL candidate mechanisms, not "the proposed mechanism". Its text also evaluates Ni-rich sulfides/pentlandite (needs >600 K), superheating of submicrometre fluffy aggregates, and nanoparticle impact vapour (~1000 K), before saying the strong Fe/Ni-carbon-oxide correlation "led us to evaluate the possibility of the carbonyl hypothesis". The Nature paper itself says only that carbonyl sublimation temperatures "are only slightly higher than that of CO2" and never prints "~100 K"; the explicit ~100 K value (intermediate between CO2 and H2O) appears in the follow-up A&A papers (Hutsemekers et al. 2021 A&A 652 L1; 2026 A&A 706 A43). Rephrased accordingly.

EVERYTHING ELSE CONFIRMED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCES:
- Date 2021-05-19 correct: both Nature papers published online 19 May 2021, same issue, back-to-back (Manfroid's own text reads "NiI lines were recently identified in the interstellar comet 2I/Borisov (Guzig & Drahus, this issue)"). ESO release eso2108 also 19 May 2021.
- Guzik & Drahus, Nature 593, 375-378 (2021). Observation dates 28, 30 and 31 January 2020 UT with VLT/X-shooter (UVB arm) CONFIRMED; mean heliocentric distance 2.322 au and geocentric 2.064 au CONFIRMED; equilibrium temperature 180 K CONFIRMED; ">700 K" normally required CONFIRMED verbatim from abstract; Q(Ni) = 0.9 +/- 0.3 x 10^22 atoms/s CONFIRMED; "0.002% relative to OH and 0.3% relative to CN" CONFIRMED verbatim; parent lifetime 340 (+260/-200) s at 1 au CONFIRMED (entry's "~340 s" fine).
- Opitom et al. 2021, A&A 650, L19: VLT/UVES, 12 epochs, 15 November 2019 to 16 March 2020 (~21 h of data), 2.1 au pre-perihelion to 2.6 au post-perihelion — ALL CONFIRMED. Fe I and Ni I both detected; log(NiI/FeI) = 0.21 +/- 0.18 for 2I vs. average -0.06 +/- 0.31 for 17 Solar System comets, i.e. "similar" — CONFIRMED, and now quantified in the corrected entry.
- Manfroid, Hutsemekers & Jehin, Nature 593, 372-374 (2021): "The spectra of about 20 different comets were collected since 2002 over a large range of heliocentric distances (0.68 to 3.25 astronomical units) with the UVES spectrograph" and "up to about 40 FeI lines and 25 NiI lines for some of them" — BOTH CONFIRMED verbatim from the ESO-hosted manuscript PDF. Abundances "of the same order of magnitude, contrasting the typical Solar System abundance ratio"; NiI/FeI on average one order of magnitude above the solar photosphere value — so the entry's "~10x more Fe in meteorites" framing is fair (ESO release: "usually there is 10 times more iron than nickel").
- Fe(CO)5 and Ni(CO)4 carbonyls CONFIRMED as named in the Nature paper, with Ni(CO)4 sublimating ~10x faster than Fe(CO)5 at ~300 K — which is the paper's own explanation for cometary Ni overabundance.
- Later 3I/ATLAS work: Hutsemekers et al., A&A 706, A43 (2026), "Pre-perihelion evolution of the NiI/FeI abundance ratio in the coma of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS: From extreme to normal" (arXiv:2509.26053, submitted 2025-09-30, revised 2025-12-17). Abstract verbatim: "comet 3I first exhibited extreme and unusual NiI/FeI abundance ratios during the initial stages of its activity. However, as its heliocentric distance decreased, this ratio became indistinguishable from those observed in Solar System comets and in comet 2I/Borisov." Spectra span 3.14-1.85 au; Ni I detected at all epochs, Fe I only below 2.64 au. So the entry's claim that 3I converged on the Borisov/SS-comet value is CONFIRMED — only the starting number was wrong.
- LOEB QUOTE IS GENUINE AND VERBATIM. Fetched https://avi-loeb.medium.com/new-data-on-the-extreme-nickel-production-of-3i-atlas-c889b20342c1 — title "New Data on the Extreme Nickel Production of 3I/ATLAS", dated October 1, 2025, contains exactly: "The interstellar comet 2I/Borisov showed nickel and iron with an abundance ratio that is similar to that observed in solar system comets." NOTHING INVENTED OR CONFLATED beyond the two items above. The loeb_take is a fair characterization: Loeb does use Borisov as the metals baseline against which he flags 3I's early nickel-heavy, iron-poor plume.

anomalies2i.title: March 2020 outburst and the transient 'double nucleus' — a textbook comet splitting event
anomalies2i.observation: Drahus et al. (ATel #13549, OGLE 1.3-m, Las Campanas) recorded two consecutive outbursts — ~0.3 mag between UT 2020 March 4.3 and 5.3 and ~0.4 mag between March 8.3 and 9.3, ~0.7 mag total in 5 days. Jewitt, Kim, Mutchler et al. (ApJL 896, L39), whose photometry independently shows a steady brightening from January 3 to February 24 indicating rising activity, tied the outburst to solids ejected with the comet outbound at ~2.8 AU: combined cross-section ~100 km^2 and ~2 × 10^7 kg in 0.1 mm grains — roughly 10^-4 of the nucleus mass for an assumed 500 m nucleus radius. HST then resolved a transient secondary on 2020-03-30 (cross-section ~0.6 km^2, dust mass ~10^5 kg). The secondary was absent in images on and before March 28 and gone again on and after April 3.
anomalies2i.loeb_take: Loeb has not treated the outburst or splitting as anomalous; both are standard comet behavior and are among the reasons he classes Borisov as a 'classical comet.' In his scale paper Borisov's coma onset and volatile-driven activity are cited as the evidence placing it in the green zone (Level 0), in direct contrast with 1I (no coma at all) and 3I (which he argues showed activity inconsistent with its spectrum).
anomalies2i.official_explanation: Jewitt et al. attribute the delayed appearance and rapid disappearance of the secondary to rotational bursting of one or more large (meter-sized) boulders under outgassing torques after ejection from the main nucleus — not a nucleus break-up. They characterize the events as 'minor events involving a negligible fraction of the total mass,' with the comet surviving the planetary region essentially intact. Outbursts and fragment shedding are common in solar-system comets.
anomalies2i.loeb_quote: In stark contrast, Borisov presented as a classical comet despite its interstellar origin
anomalies2i.quote_source: Eldadi, Tenenbaum & Loeb, 'The Loeb Scale: Astronomical Classification of Interstellar Objects', arXiv:2508.09167, 2025-08
anomalies2i._verifyNotes: One minor misattribution, everything else verified. (1) The "steady rise in activity from January 3 to February 24" was attributed to Drahus et al. ATel #13549, but ATel #13549 contains no January/February dates (it reports only the two March outbursts, with monitoring since mid-December 2019). The Jan 3 - Feb 24 steady brightening is from Jewitt et al.'s own photometry in ApJL 896 L39 ("the data show a steady brightening from January 3 to February 24, indicating a period of increasing activity"). Observation text reworded to attribute it correctly, and the two outburst magnitudes made precise (0.3 mag March 4.3-5.3, 0.4 mag March 8.3-9.3, per the ATel verbatim). (2) All other facts confirmed against primary sources: HST secondary on 2020-03-30, absent on/before Mar 28 and on/after Apr 3; ~2.8 AU outbound; ~100 km^2 cross-section; ~2e7 kg in 0.1 mm grains; fractional mass lost ~1e-4 of a 500-m-radius nucleus; secondary ~0.6 km^2 and ~1e5 kg; mechanism verbatim "rotational bursting of one or more large (meter-sized) boulders under the action of outgassing torques, following their ejection from the main nucleus"; closing quote verbatim "minor events involving a negligible fraction of the total mass: 2I/Borisov will survive its passage through the planetary region largely unscathed." (3) Loeb quote verified verbatim in arXiv:2508.09167 PDF: "In stark contrast, Borisov presented as a classical comet despite its interstellar origin (Guzik et al., 2020)." Borisov = Level 0 in the green zone; 1I/'Oumuamua and 3I/ATLAS both Level 4; paper cites Borisov's coma at 2.8 AU consistent with water-ice sublimation plus CN/C2 volatiles — matching the loeb_take. loeb_scale: 0 is correct. (4) Added ATel #13549 URL to sources; changed "meter-scale" to "meter-sized" to match the paper's wording.

anomalies2i.title: 'May be the first truly pristine comet ever observed' — anomalously high, spatially uniform polarization
anomalies2i.observation: Bagnulo et al. (Nature Communications 12, 1797) imaged Borisov in polarimetric mode with VLT/FORS2 from 2019-12-25 to 2020-03-20. Measured coma polarization Pr (R_SPECIAL filter) fell from 3.76 ± 0.08% at phase angle 28.48 deg (2019-12-25) through 1.19 ± 0.21% at 24.14 deg (2020-02-06) to -0.82 ± 0.13% at 18.06 deg (2020-03-20), with V- and I-filter values consistent (e.g. V: 3.35 ± 0.07% at 28.48 deg) — systematically higher than typical solar-system comets at matching phase angles. The only solar-system object with a comparable polarimetric curve is C/1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp), and unlike Hale-Bopp (whose polarimetric images showed jets and arcs), Borisov's coma is polarimetrically homogeneous.
anomalies2i.loeb_take: Loeb does not contest this result and has not framed Borisov's dust as anomalous in the technosignature sense. His consistent public position is that Borisov is the natural interstellar comet against which 1I and 3I should be judged — pristine but ordinary in kind. No Borisov-specific Loeb quote on the polarimetry exists; his general characterization is that Borisov 'appeared familiar', and his Loeb-scale paper (arXiv:2508.09167) rates Borisov Level 0 versus Level 4 for both 1I/'Oumuamua and 3I/ATLAS.
anomalies2i.official_explanation: ESO and the authors read the high, uniform polarization as evidence of an unprocessed, compositionally homogeneous dust population: Borisov apparently never passed close to any star before its 2019 solar passage, so its grains were never thermally or radiatively altered — making it more pristine than Hale-Bopp, which had made one prior solar passage (~2250 BCE). Co-author Alberto Cellino's polarization-plus-color analysis concluded the formation environment was not so different in composition from the early Solar System.
anomalies2i.loeb_quote: Among the four interstellar objects, only Borisov appeared familiar.
anomalies2i.quote_source: Avi Loeb, 'The Unfamiliar Nature of Interstellar Objects', Medium, Sep 2022 — https://avi-loeb.medium.com/the-unfamiliar-nature-of-interstellar-objects-de8c855677e4
anomalies2i._verifyNotes: Minor corrections only; core entry is accurate. (1) Title fixed: the paper hedges — abstract says Borisov "may" be the first truly pristine comet ever observed; original title-quote dropped the "may". (2) Observation clarified: the three cited Pr values are specifically the R_SPECIAL-filter measurements from Table 1 (V and I filters were also measured; e.g. V gives 3.35 +/- 0.07% at 28.48 deg and -1.05 +/- 0.15% at 18.06 deg). All three quoted values verified verbatim against Table 1 with correct dates and phase angles. (3) Publication date 2021-03-30 exact (Nat Commun 12:1797; ESO eso2106 same day). (4) Loeb side verified: Borisov = Level 0 in arXiv:2508.09167 (1I=4, 3I=4); the "appeared familiar" phrasing is genuine, from Loeb's Sep 2022 Medium essay "The Unfamiliar Nature of Interstellar Objects" — added as loeb_quote with source. (5) Official explanation fairly stated: ESO release confirms pristine/never-passed-a-star interpretation, Hale-Bopp's single prior solar passage (~2250 BCE per paper), and the Cellino polarization-plus-color quote ("not so different in composition from the environment in the early Solar System"). Nothing invented or conflated.

anomalies2i.title: Compact sub-kilometre nucleus — small, ordinary, and tightly bracketed
anomalies2i.observation: Jewitt, Hui, Kim et al. (arXiv:1912.05422, published ApJL 888, L23) modelled HST high-resolution imaging and found the scattering is dominated by a coma of large particles (characteristic size ~0.1 mm) ejected anisotropically. Convolution modelling of the coma surface-brightness profile sets a robust upper limit of spherical-equivalent nucleus radius rn <= 0.5 km (geometric albedo 0.04 assumed); an independent constraint from the measured non-gravitational acceleration gives rn > 0.2 km (density 500 kg m^-3 assumed). So 0.2 km < rn <= 0.5 km, i.e. a few hundred metres.
anomalies2i.loeb_take: Loeb accepts the sub-kilometre nucleus at face value and uses it purely as a scale reference: he describes Borisov's nucleus as 'about a few hundred meters in radius,' and in his 3I/ATLAS essays states that 3I's nucleus is roughly a thousand times more massive than Borisov's and about a million times more massive than 1I/'Oumuamua. For Borisov the size is a datum, not an anomaly.
anomalies2i.official_explanation: A few-hundred-metre icy nucleus with a large-grain, anisotropically ejected dust coma is entirely typical of active solar-system comets; the non-gravitational acceleration is fully accounted for by measured outgassing (unlike 1I/'Oumuamua, where acceleration occurred with no detected coma). Independent estimates (e.g. Hui et al. 2020; VISIR thermal work) converge on the same few-hundred-metre range.
anomalies2i.loeb_quote: about a few hundred meters in radius
anomalies2i.quote_source: Avi Loeb, 'The Unfamiliar Nature of Interstellar Objects,' Medium, 2022-09-23
anomalies2i._verifyNotes: All claims verified against primary sources. (1) Date 2019-12-11 is the exact arXiv v1 submission date of 1912.05422 (ApJL publication 2020-01-13). (2) All numbers match the abstract verbatim: 0.1 mm characteristic particle size, anisotropic ejection, coma convolution modelling upper limit rn < 0.5 km at albedo 0.04, non-gravitational lower limit rn > 0.2 km at density 500 kg/m^3; journal ref ApJL 888, L23 (2020) and author list confirmed via IOPscience. Sole nit: abstract writes the upper limit as strict '<' rather than '<='; immaterial. (3) Quote 'about a few hundred meters in radius' appears verbatim in Loeb's Medium essay 'The Unfamiliar Nature of Interstellar Objects', confirmed published Sep 23, 2022; the loeb_take's 3I/ATLAS ratios (thousand x Borisov, million x 'Oumuamua) match Loeb's 2025 anomalies essays. (4) Official explanation is fairly stated and backed by real work: Hui et al. 2020 (AJ) independently derived a most-likely ~0.4 km radius from non-gravitational acceleration, and VLT/VISIR thermal characterization (Bolin et al., EPSC 2020) exists, converging on the few-hundred-metre range. (5) Nothing invented or conflated. No changes needed.

notes2i:
DASHBOARD FRAMING — 2I/Borisov is the control case and the file is intentionally thin (5 entries, all Loeb-scale 0).

VERIFIED BASELINE FACTS (safe to render as fixed context, not anomalies):
- Discovered 2019-08-30 by Gennadiy Borisov (Crimea), MPC designation C/2019 Q4; some Loeb essays date the detection 2019-08-29.
- Perihelion 2019-12-08 at q = 2.006–2.007 AU; eccentricity e = 3.356.
- Second confirmed interstellar object; first with unambiguous cometary activity.

LOEB-SCALE ANCHOR (the single most useful cross-object number): in Loeb's August 2025 "Interstellar Object Significance Scale" (IOSS, arXiv:2508.09167), a 0–10 framework extending the Torino Scale — Levels 0–3 natural, 4–7 progressively anomalous, 8–10 confirmed artificial — the retroactive rankings are 1I/'Oumuamua = Level 4, 2I/Borisov = Level 0, 3I/ATLAS = Level 4. Borisov is the only interstellar object Loeb has scored at 0. Recommend showing this as a three-object bar on the dashboard.

QUOTE CONFIDENCE:
- HIGH (clean HTML fetch, verbatim): the two Medium quotes (2022-09-23 "only Borisov appeared familiar…"; 2025-10-01 "…nickel and iron with an abundance ratio that is similar to that observed in solar system comets."); Bagnulo's "2I/Borisov could represent the first truly pristine comet ever observed" (ESO release eso2106, 2021-03-30 — not used as a loeb_quote but good for a discoverer callout on B-04).
- MEDIUM (extracted from a PDF via summarizer, returned inside quote marks): the B-03 Loeb quote "In stark contrast, Borisov presented as a classical comet despite its interstellar origin" from arXiv:2508.09167. Treat as near-verbatim; if the dashboard needs bulletproof wording, swap in the 2022 Medium quote.
- B-04 has NO Borisov-specific Loeb quote — left empty deliberately rather than fabricated.

CONTRADICTION TO PRESERVE, NOT SMOOTH OVER (B-01): the two CO measurements disagree in magnitude — Bodewits/HST-COS gives CO/H2O >= 173%, Cordiner/ALMA gives 35–105%. Different techniques, different epochs, different assumed water rates. Both conclude "most CO-rich comet observed inside ~2.5 AU." Show both bars side by side rather than averaging.

THE B-02 PAIRING IS THE LOAD-BEARING ITEM FOR THE 3I/ATLAS DASHBOARD: Guzik & Drahus (Nature 593, 375) and Manfroid, Hutsemékers & Jehin (Nature 593, 372) published in the SAME issue on 2021-05-19, with a joint ESO release (eso2108). That simultaneity is the whole point — the "exotic" interstellar metal vapor was shown to be universal cometary chemistry on the same day it was announced. Follow-on VLT work (A&A, arXiv:2509.26053 and arXiv:2605.07652) tracks 3I/ATLAS's Ni I/Fe I from log ≈ 1.5 at 2.64 AU down to log ≈ 0.3 near 2 AU, at which point it is "indistinguishable" from solar-system comets and from 2I/Borisov. Solar reference: log10(Ni/Fe) = −1.25 ± 0.04.
